t: Introduction: aim of the topic and outline
n: In this topic we study the examination of living persons. Examination of living persons is the type most often carried out in practice, and it is ordered in criminal, civil and administrative cases. The examination is carried out in the outpatient department of a forensic medical institution, and also in district, city and inter-district departments. If the necessary conditions exist, it can also be carried out in a medical institution. The procedure is determined by the Criminal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Civil Code, the Law on Forensic Examination and the Instruction. Lesson outline: bodily injuries, state of health and malingering, sexual conditions, sexual crimes, and then the procedure for carrying out the examination.

Now let us consider when an examination is ordered. These are the most frequently performed examinations, and they are ordered in criminal, civil and administrative cases. The cases in which it is ordered fall into four groups. The first is bodily injuries, in which the nature and degree of severity of the injury are determined. The second is sexual conditions: sex, virginity, sexual maturity, reproductive ability, pregnancy, delivery and abortion. The third is sexual crimes, that is, rape, sodomy and lewd acts. The fourth is the state of health, in which simulation, aggravation, artificial disease, self-mutilation and age are established.

Examination of bodily injuries is carried out in accordance with the Criminal Code and the rules for determining the degree of severity. Data on these questions must be recorded in the expert's conclusion. The expert resolves five questions. First, the type and site of the injury. Second, the weapon or means of infliction. Third, the mechanism of origin. Fourth, the age of the injury. Fifth, the degree of severity, that is, the degree and the qualifying feature. Remember: the degree of severity is always determined with indication of the qualifying feature.

Now the legal classification of bodily injuries. According to the Code injuries are of three kinds: grave, which is Article 104, of moderate severity, which is Article 105, and slight, which is Article 109. Under Article 104 an injury is considered grave if it is dangerous to life or has caused loss of not less than 33% of working capacity. In an injury of moderate severity health is impaired for more than 21 days or the loss is from 10% to 33%. Under Article 109 slight injuries are of two kinds. In the first health is impaired for more than 6 days but not more than 21 days, with a loss of up to 10%. In the second the impairment is up to 6 days, with no persistent loss.

t: Criteria for determining the degree of severity
n: The criteria for determining the degree of severity are the medical characterisation of the qualifying features of the Criminal Code. They are applied in criminal, civil and administrative cases. There are seven criteria: danger to life, duration of impairment of health, persistent loss, loss of an organ, mental disorder, termination of pregnancy and disfigurement. The presence of one of the criteria is sufficient. If there are several criteria, the degree is determined by the more severe criterion. Attention, there is a risk of error: a clinically grave condition and forensic medical grave bodily harm are not the same. Their aims and criteria differ, so the results may not coincide.

Let us consider injuries dangerous to life. Injuries that directly threaten life at the moment of infliction are considered dangerous to life. An injury that has led to a life-threatening state which the body cannot restore by itself is also regarded as grave. An important rule: even if medical care has removed the threat, the injury is still assessed as dangerous to life. The groups are as follows: head and trunk, with fracture of the skull bones and injury of an internal organ; large vessels, that is, the aorta, carotid and femoral arteries; a degree III burn over 15% of the body; and also a life-threatening state, that is, severe shock and coma of degree II-III.

We consolidate the topic with these quick questions. Let us list the criteria once more: danger to life, duration of impairment of health, persistent loss, function of an organ, termination of pregnancy, mental disorder and disfigurement. First question: how many degrees of severity of injury are there? Answer: grave, of moderate severity, slight with short-term impairment, and slight. Second question: is clinical severity equal to forensic medical severity? Answer: no, the aims and criteria differ, and the results may not coincide. Third question: what if there are several criteria? Answer: one criterion is sufficient, and if there are several, assessment is by the criterion corresponding to the more severe degree.

Working capacity is general or professional. General working capacity means self-care and simple work, professional relates to a particular profession. In assessment only the general is taken. Temporary loss is expressed in days, persistent in percentage. If the loss lasts more than 120 days, it is considered conditionally persistent. Degrees of persistent loss: 33+ percent grave, 10-33 percent moderate, up to 10 percent slight, short-term. Another rule: fracture of the humerus, femur and tibia leads to a loss of more than 1/3, so this is considered a grave injury.

The duration of impairment of health is the most often used criterion. It means a disturbance of function that has caused temporary incapacity for work. The limits are as follows: up to 6 days slight, 6-21 days slight short-term, 21+ days moderate. Attention: the duration of impairment of health is not equal to the duration of treatment or of anatomical recovery. A period prolonged because of late presentation, diseases or deficiencies of medical care is not counted. That is, the expert assesses only the period that depends on the injury itself.

t: Loss of sight, speech and hearing
n: Now loss of sight, speech and hearing. If in both eyes there is permanent total blindness or visual acuity of 0.04 or less, the injury is regarded as grave. With complete loss of sight in one eye, more than 1/3 of working capacity is lost, and this too is a grave injury. Grave injury also includes complete loss or loss of half of the tongue and deafness of both ears. Attention: deafness of both ears is not the same as deafness of one ear. The first is grave, whereas loss of hearing of one ear is regarded as an injury of moderate severity.

t: Loss of an organ and termination of pregnancy
n: Let us consider loss of an organ and termination of pregnancy. Separation of an arm or leg from the body, or persistent loss of function such as paralysis, counts as loss of an organ; the hand or foot is equated to it. Loss of reproductive ability, and also loss of one testis, ovary or kidney, is likewise a grave bodily injury. Termination of pregnancy is called grave if after trauma a stillborn or non-viable infant is born and the connection is direct. If a viable infant is born or an ectopic pregnancy is terminated, severity is determined by other criteria.

On mental disorder and irremovable disfigurement. Assessment of mental disorder is carried out in five steps: is there a mental disorder, was there no disorder before, is a corresponding injury identified, is there a direct causal connection. If the answers are yes, the conclusion is grave injury. The commission includes a forensic psychiatrist or psychiatrist; if necessary, a neurologist and neurosurgeon are also involved. The presence of disfigurement is determined by the court, whereas the examination assesses whether it is removable or irremovable. An irremovable mark does not disappear by itself and requires surgery; a cosmetologist and plastic surgeon take part here.

We recall the rules for applying the criteria. To determine the degree of severity the presence of one of the medical criteria is sufficient. If there are several criteria, the more severe is taken. If there are many injuries in one incident, an overall degree is determined. Injuries of different age are assessed separately. In a person with a previous illness only the consequences causally connected with the new injury are taken into account. Exceptions: deterioration because of age, disease, late presentation and deficiencies of treatment is not taken into account. If the nature or consequence is indefinite, the degree is not established.

t: Case analysis: severity of a bodily injury
n: Now a case analysis. Situation: a single eye, healthy before the injury, was removed after being damaged. What is the degree of severity of the injury? Answer: the assessment is made by the criterion of persistent loss of general working capacity. The loss is more than a third, so the injury is grave. Attention, there is a risk of error: if an eye that had no vision is lost, the degree is determined by the duration of impairment of health. Remember also: clinical and forensic medical assessment are not the same, their aims and criteria differ, and the results may not coincide.

t: Examination to determine the state of health
n: Examination to determine the state of health is ordered in several cases: inability to attend a summons because of a doubtful illness, participation of a suspect in investigative and court actions, and determining whether detention is possible. It is also ordered for deferment of execution of a sentence, that is, in illness, pregnancy and delivery, and in evasion of military service. It is usually carried out by a commission with clinician-specialists: medical documents are studied, and sometimes inpatient examination is needed. The commission also takes into account the possibility of simulation, aggravation, that is, exaggeration of illness, dissimulation, that is, concealment, artificial disease and self-mutilation.

Simulation is when a healthy person presents himself as having a non-existent illness. The simulator presents his state as more severe, and his complaints do not match the objective signs. To establish it the person is observed for a long time; some examinations are carried out suddenly and repeatedly. Examples of methods: in gastric ulcer, blood and ascorbic acid are added to the faeces. In heart disease, strong tea and coffee cause tachycardia. In pulmonary tuberculosis, the sputum and X-ray of a real patient are used. In pulmonary haemorrhage, blood from the gums or nose is mixed into the sputum.

Aggravation is exaggeration of the signs of an existing illness or trauma. It may be deliberate or pathological, with the aim of escaping punishment or evading service. Dissimulation, by contrast, is the opposite of simulation: deliberate concealment of an illness or pathological state. It is always deliberate, the reason being the demands of a profession or evasion of responsibility. Attention: simulation and dissimulation are not the same. One shows an illness that does not exist, the other conceals one that does.

We divide artificial diseases into three groups. Skin: tight binding of a limb or light blows give artificial oedema; if paraffin, Vaseline or fat is injected under the skin, an artificial tumour appears. Artificial dermatitis arises from mechanical, chemical or thermal action; if kerosene, turpentine or saliva is injected under the skin, abscess and phlegmon develop. Internal organs: a lot of laxative and soap solution give gastroenteritis; a lot of table salt gives nephrosonephritis; ephedrine gives signs of hypertensive disease. Eye and ear: rubbing, dust or acid cause conjunctivitis and keratitis; a foreign body is inserted into the ear, and the tympanic membrane is perforated with a piercing object.

Self-mutilation is deliberate infliction of injury on oneself for a particular purpose. It is often encountered in evasion of military service. The injury is more often on the arm and leg, mainly on the hand, that is, where the person can reach with his own hand. Signs: several superficial wounds near the main injury, that is, repeated action; amputation of fingers at different levels, if accidental then at one level; injury mainly on the left; the type of weapon is piercing-cutting or firearm, sometimes a blunt object. An investigative experiment is recommended: the person's account is tested under conditions close to the incident.

Case analysis. Situation: a conscript has, on the hand near the main injury, several superficial incised wounds and amputation of fingers at different levels. The injury is mainly on the left hand. The person explains it as an accident. Recall the difference: in simulation a healthy person feigns a non-existent illness, whereas in self-mutilation a real injury is inflicted on oneself. Question: do the signs fit an accident or self-injury? Answer: the set of signs points to self-mutilation; an investigative experiment is recommended.

An examination to determine sex is needed when sex has been wrongly determined, when issuing a document, in annulment of marriage or in criminal investigation. Hermaphroditism is the simultaneous presence of genital organs characteristic of two sexes. True and false types are distinguished. In the true type male and female glands are present together. In the false male there is a testis, that is, spermatogenesis, but woman-like features occur. In the false female there is an ovary, that is, oogenesis, but there are man-like features. The examination uses history, medical documents, anthropometry, clinical and laboratory examination and chromosome analysis.

Sexual maturity is the level of development that makes it possible to lead a sexual life without harm to health. Usually those under 14 years are considered sexually immature. The question of determining maturity arises in the interval from 14 years to marriageable age. In girls body length standing should be not less than 150 cm, sitting not less than 80 cm. Chest circumference at rest should be not less than 78–80 cm. Pelvic dimensions at least: distance between the anterior superior iliac spines 26–27 cm, between the greater trochanters 29 cm, external conjugate 17–18 cm. In women maturity covers the ability to have sexual intercourse, pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding.

Virginity is determined mainly by the anatomical integrity of the hymen. The hymen is a duplication of the vaginal mucosa, in which the base, free edge and opening are distinguished. Usually deflowering occurs at first intercourse; the hymen may also be disrupted by a finger, an object or in an operation. The forms fall into three groups. The first group is the usual: annular, semilunar and tubular. The second group is the unusual: lobed, spiral, serrated. The third group is very rare: two-windowed, septate and imperforate.

t: Healing periods of a hymenal tear
n: Let us consider the healing periods of a hymenal tear. In thin, elastic hymens tears heal faster than in thick, fleshy ones. At first there are bleeding, swelling and a clot. Then the swelling decreases and a whitish coating appears. By the end of week 1 granulation, within 2-3 weeks a scar forms. After 3 weeks the age cannot be established. The tear is usually in the lower segment, between 5 and 7 o'clock; a natural notch may be in any segment. Attention: a tear and a notch are not the same. The notch does not reach the base and its edge is normal; the edge of an old tear is thick and scarred.

Quick questions. First question: what is the difference between true and false hermaphroditism? In the true type there are glands of both sexes, in the false type a gland of one sex, while the external features resemble the other sex. Second question: up to what age is a person usually considered sexually immature? Answer: those under 14 are regarded as immature. Third question: are pelvic and body dimensions a strict criterion? No, they have relative significance; even with smaller values a woman can safely bear a child. Attention, risk of error: a tear in the hymen is not a natural notch. A tear is more often in the lower segment, between 5 and 7 on the clock face. A natural notch most often does not reach the base.

Reproductive ability is understood differently in man and woman. In a man it means the ability to have sexual intercourse and to fertilise, in a woman the ability to have sexual intercourse, become pregnant and give birth. In a man impotence is related to diseases of the central nervous system, malformations of the external genitalia and endocrine diseases. The fertilising ability is determined by laboratory examination of the ejaculate; if motile normal spermatozoa are found, the ability is confirmed. In a woman atresia of the vagina, aplasia, scars, tumours and vaginismus hinder intercourse. A narrow pelvis and deformity of the pelvic bones hinder natural delivery.

t: Determination of pregnancy and previous delivery
n: Determination of pregnancy and previous delivery. In an ongoing pregnancy menstruation stops, the mammary glands enlarge and pigmentation increases. In the laboratory chorionic gonadotropin is determined. Reliable signs: on auscultation the fetal heartbeat, and on palpation and ultrasound the parts and movement of the fetus. In the first days after delivery the breasts are swollen, the areola is darker, there is discharge, and the perineum is wide. In a woman who has given birth the external os of the cervix is slit-like, in one who has not usually round.

t: Types of abortion and criminal abortion
n: Abortion is termination of pregnancy before 22 weeks; it is spontaneous or artificial. There are three types. Spontaneous abortion arises from illness or poisoning. Medical abortion is performed by an obstetrician-gynaecologist: up to 12 weeks on request, thereafter on indications. Criminal abortion is performed by an untrained person, which is Article 114 of the Criminal Code. With the mechanical method abrasions, bruises and wounds are found; with the chemical method signs of burn and poisoning. Air embolism, shock, acute haemorrhage, perforation and infection may be the cause of death.

t: Case analysis: examination of sexual conditions
n: Case analysis. Situation: outside a medical institution, a person without medical training terminated a woman's pregnancy; the woman has acute haemorrhage. The examination establishes: whether there was pregnancy and its termination, by what method the pregnancy was terminated, and what the consequences are. On examination, traces corresponding to the method are sought: abrasions, bruises, wounds and burns on the external genitalia, vagina and uterus. Question: how does this case differ from a medical abortion, and which article provides for liability?

Rape. Article 118 of the Criminal Code: sexual intercourse against the will with violence, threat or by taking advantage of helplessness. Marks of violence are on the inner surface of the thighs and genitalia as bruises and abrasions; a threat, however, leaves no marks. Semen is sought in the vagina, on the pubis, in the perineum and on the thighs; the earlier the swab is taken, the more effective it is. The examination proceeds in five stages: the document, that is, the order, record, medical documents; the interview, that is, gynaecological history; the examination, in which injuries and signs of helplessness are sought; the samples, that is, swabs and imprints; the laboratory, in which semen, blood and hair are examined.

Sodomy and lewd acts. Article 120 provides for sexual intercourse of a man with a man without violence; both the active and the passive participant are liable. In the active participant the penis and pubic region are examined, and blood, hair, faeces and an oily substance are sought; in the coronal sulcus they persist for long. In the passive participant the anus and rectum are examined, and abrasions, haemorrhages and fissures are found; with regular intercourse the sphincter weakens. Attention: diseases such as proctitis and haemorrhoids may be wrongly interpreted as a sign of passive sodomy. Lewd acts against a person under 16 years is Article 129. Sometimes no marks remain.

t: Passive participant: signs of regular intercourse
n: In the passive participant the findings depend on the regularity of intercourse. In passive participants abrasions, haemorrhages and fissures are found in the anal and rectal region. With few acts of intercourse, in an adult passive participant sometimes no injury or change is found. With regular intercourse the anus is funnel-shaped and depressed, the sphincter is weakened and the opening gapes. With regular intercourse the radial folds of the anus are smoothed; the mucosa of the lower rectum also changes.

t: Venereal diseases and transmission of HIV infection
n: Venereal diseases and transmission of HIV infection. Article 113: a person who, knowing that he has a venereal disease or HIV, that is, human immunodeficiency virus, or AIDS, has infected another or put another at risk is liable. Attention: this crime belongs not to crimes against sexual freedom but to the group of crimes dangerous to life or health; that is the difference from rape. The examination is carried out with the participation of dermatovenereologists and AIDS specialists: examination, clinical and laboratory investigation, analysis of medical documents, source of infection. A person found to have a late stage of the disease is a subject of the crime. A medical worker who infected with HIV through improper performance of duty is also liable.

Case analysis. Situation: a woman presented with suspected rape. There is a bruise on the inner surface of the thigh, and semen may be present in the vagina. A vaginal swab and imprints from the pubis, perineum and thigh are taken as quickly as possible. With time the probability of finding spermatozoa decreases. Semen usually persists in the vagina for up to 3-5 days, so the sooner the sample is taken, the more reliable the result. Question: should the suspect be examined? Traces of defence and blood or hair belonging to the woman may be found on him.

t: General algorithm of conducting the examination
n: The examination of living persons is carried out by a general algorithm, in six stages. The methodology is determined by the features of the incident and the task set before the examination, so each type is distinctive. The circumstances of the event are first studied from the data of the order or ruling appointing the examination. Then the medical documents are reviewed. Then the person is interviewed and examined. After that special investigations are carried out and finally the expert's conclusion is drawn up.

Procedure of examination and participants. The person is identified by a document: passport, military ID or certificate; in sexual cases two photographs are also needed. The examination is carried out with a ruler, magnifier and stereomicroscope; if necessary, specialists examine together. Photographing an injury is possible only with the person's permission. Participants: for minors, parents or teachers; for persons lacking capacity, the legal representative; if the person is of the other sex and undressing is needed, the investigator leaves the room; for a patient under treatment, the person who ordered the examination or a representative and the treating doctor take part.

t: Interview and examination: what is studied
n: Let us consider what is studied in the interview and examination. In examination of bodily injuries the interview establishes when, where, by whom, with what, on which region of the body and how many times the action occurred. The condition after the injury and recourse to medical care are asked about; the interview ends with the complaints at the time of examination. At examination the type, site, shape, size, colour, contamination of the injury and the state of the surrounding skin are studied. For an abrasion the crust and its level are described, for a wound the edges, ends, walls and base. Photographing is done with the person's permission.

Structure of the expert's conclusion. When all investigations are complete, the conclusion is drawn up; in it all investigations carried out and their results are documented. In the findings, answers are given to the questions put to the examination. In bodily injuries the type of injury, site, features, injuring weapon, mechanism of origin and age of the injury are stated. The degree of severity is given with the qualifying feature, that is, danger to life, duration of impairment of health or persistent loss. At the end photographs and diagrams are appended.

We conclude the topic. Remember: the examination proceeds in six stages: the circumstances, the medical document, the interview, the examination, additional investigation and the conclusion. Attention: the duration of impairment of health is not exactly equal to the duration of treatment; late presentation or a deficiency of treatment is not counted. Limits: up to 6 days slight; from 6 to 21 days short-term slight; more than 21 days of moderate severity. Independent work: draw up a six-stage plan for a given case and write who takes part at each stage.
